amc12-ahsme-1972-01.title: Scale to integers
amc12-ahsme-1972-01.body:
Double II to get $8,15,17$, a Pythagorean triple. Double IV to get $7,9,11$: $49+81=130\neq121$. I ($3,4,5$) and III ($7,24,25$) are well-known triples.

**Answer: (D) I, II, and III**

amc12-ahsme-1972-03.title: Find the quadratic
amc12-ahsme-1972-03.body:
$x$ is a root of $x^2-x+1=0$ (sum of roots $1$, product $\frac{1+3}{4}=1$). So $x^2-x=-1$ and $\frac1{x^2-x}=-1$.

**Answer: (B) $-1$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-04.title: Free choices
amc12-ahsme-1972-04.body:
$X$ must contain $1$ and $2$; each of $3,4,5$ is in or out freely: $2^3=8$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

amc12-ahsme-1972-07.title: Pick numbers
amc12-ahsme-1972-07.body:
Take $yz=1$, $zx=2$, $xy=3$. Multiplying, $(xyz)^2=6$, so $xyz=\sqrt6$ and $x=\sqrt6$, $y=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}$, $z=\frac{\sqrt6}{3}$. Then $\frac{x}{yz}=\sqrt6$ and $\frac{y}{zx}=\frac{\sqrt6}{4}$, a ratio of $4:1$.

**Answer: (E) 4:1**

amc12-ahsme-1972-08.title: Square both sides
amc12-ahsme-1972-08.body:
Both sides are nonnegative, so square: $x^2-2x\log y+\log^2y=x^2+2x\log y+\log^2y$, i.e. $4x\log y=0$. So $x=0$ or $\log y=0$ (i.e. $y=1$), which is $x(y-1)=0$.

**Answer: (D) $x(y-1)=0$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-08.title: Two cases
amc12-ahsme-1972-08.body:
If $x\ge\log y$: $x-\log y=x+\log y\Rightarrow\log y=0\Rightarrow y=1$. If $x<\log y$: $\log y-x=x+\log y\Rightarrow x=0$. Either way $x=0$ or $y=1$.

**Answer: (D) $x(y-1)=0$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-09.title: Two equations
amc12-ahsme-1972-09.body:
Let a box have $S$ sheets and $E$ envelopes. Ann: $S=E+50$. Sue: $S=3(E-50)$. So $E+50=3E-150$, $E=100$, $S=150$.

**Answer: (A) 150**

amc12-ahsme-1972-09.title: Test the choices
amc12-ahsme-1972-09.body:
If $S=150$ then $E=100$ (Ann). Sue writes $50$ letters using $150$ sheets and $50$ envelopes, leaving $50$ envelopes ✓.

**Answer: (A) 150**

amc12-ahsme-1972-10.title: Distance
amc12-ahsme-1972-10.body:
$|x-2|$ is the distance from $x$ to $2$; it must be between $1$ and $7$. To the right: $3\le x\le9$; to the left: $-5\le x\le1$.

**Answer: (D)**

amc12-ahsme-1972-11.title: Eliminate $x^2$
amc12-ahsme-1972-11.body:
Subtract: $y^2+3y-28=0$, so $y=4$ or $y=-7$. But $x^2=3y-12$ must be $\ge0$, so $y\ge4$; $y=-7$ fails. With $y=4$, $x=0$ works in both.

**Answer: (A) 4 only**

amc12-ahsme-1972-11.title: Geometry
amc12-ahsme-1972-11.body:
The first is the circle of radius $4$, so $|y|\le4$. The second is the parabola $y=\frac{x^2+12}{3}\ge4$. They can only meet where $y=4$: at $(0,4)$.

**Answer: (A) 4 only**

amc12-ahsme-1972-12.title: Convert units
amc12-ahsme-1972-12.body:
Let the edge be $s$ feet $=12s$ inches. Volume $s^3$ cubic feet; surface $6(12s)^2=864s^2$ square inches. $s^3=864s^2\Rightarrow s=864$.

**Answer: (B) 864**

amc12-ahsme-1972-13.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1972-13.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $D=(0,12)$, $B=(12,0)$, $E=(5,12)$. Then $M=(2.5,6)$ and the bisector has direction $(12,-5)$ (perpendicular to $AE=(5,12)$). Points on it: $(2.5+12t,\ 6-5t)$. $P$ ($x=0$): $t=-\frac{5}{24}$. $Q$ ($x=12$): $t=\frac{19}{24}$. Distances from $M$ are proportional to $|t|$: $PM:MQ=5:19$.

**Answer: (C) 5:19**

amc12-ahsme-1972-13.title: Similar triangles via horizontal distances
amc12-ahsme-1972-13.body:
Along line $PQ$, lengths are proportional to horizontal distances. $P$ is at $x=0$, $M$ at $x=\frac52$ (midpoint of $A$ and $E$), $Q$ at $x=12$. So $PM:MQ=\frac52:\frac{19}2=5:19$.

**Answer: (C) 5:19**

amc12-ahsme-1972-14.title: Drop an altitude
amc12-ahsme-1972-14.body:
Call the vertices $A$ ($30^\circ$), $B$ ($45^\circ$), $C$ ($105^\circ$); $AC=8$. Drop the altitude from $C$ to $AB$: in the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle at $A$, it has length $\frac{8}{2}=4$. In the $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle at $B$, $BC=4\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (B) $4\sqrt2$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-15.title: Rate equation
amc12-ahsme-1972-15.body:
With $N$ bricks, the rates are $\frac N9$ and $\frac N{10}$. Together: $5\left(\frac N9+\frac N{10}-10\right)=N$, so $\frac{19N}{18}-50=N$, $\frac N{18}=50$, $N=900$.

**Answer: (C) 900**

amc12-ahsme-1972-15.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1972-15.body:
$900$ bricks: rates $100$ and $90$ per hour, together $190-10=180$ per hour, $900\div180=5$ hours ✓.

**Answer: (C) 900**

amc12-ahsme-1972-17.title: Lengths
amc12-ahsme-1972-17.body:
Take length $1$ and $x\ge1$. The shorter piece $s$ must satisfy $1-s\ge xs$, i.e. $s\le\frac1{x+1}$. The cut must be within $\frac1{x+1}$ of one of the ends: total favourable length $\frac{2}{x+1}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{2}{x+1}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-17.title: Check special values
amc12-ahsme-1972-17.body:
For $x=1$ the event is certain, and (E) gives $1$. For $x=3$ the shorter piece must be at most $\frac14$, so the cut lies in one of the two outer quarters: probability $\frac12=\frac{2}{3+1}$ ✓, while (D) would give $\frac13$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{2}{x+1}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-18.title: Similar triangles
amc12-ahsme-1972-18.body:
$AB\parallel DC$, so $\triangle EAB\sim\triangle ECD$ with ratio $AB:CD=2:1$. Thus $AE:EC=2:1$ and $EC=\frac13\cdot11=3\frac23$.

**Answer: (A) $3\frac23$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-18.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1972-18.body:
Let $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,0)$, $D=(p,h)$, $C=(p+1,h)$. Lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at height $\frac{2h}{3}$, i.e. $\frac23$ of the way from $A$ to $C$. So $EC=\frac{11}3$.

**Answer: (A) $3\frac23$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-20.title: Right triangle
amc12-ahsme-1972-20.body:
Draw a right triangle with legs $2ab$ (opposite) and $a^2-b^2$ (adjacent). The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{4a^2b^2+(a^2-b^2)^2}=a^2+b^2$. So $\sin x=\frac{2ab}{a^2+b^2}$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1972-20.title: Half-angle view
amc12-ahsme-1972-20.body:
With $\tan t=\frac ba$, $\tan2t=\frac{2ab}{a^2-b^2}$, so $x=2t$ and $\sin x=\frac{2\tan t}{1+\tan^2t}=\frac{2ab}{a^2+b^2}$.

**Answer: (E)**

amc12-ahsme-1972-21.title: Split at a crossing
amc12-ahsme-1972-21.body:
The figure is the closed path $A\to C\to E\to F\to B\to D\to A$. Let $P$ be where $AC$ crosses $BD$.
- In triangle $APD$: $\angle A+\angle D=180^\circ-\angle APD$.
- $PCEFB$ is a pentagon (angle sum $540^\circ$) whose angle at $P$ is the reflex angle $360^\circ-\angle BPC$. So $\angle B+\angle C+\angle E+\angle F=540^\circ-(360^\circ-\angle BPC)=180^\circ+\angle BPC$.

Since $\angle BPC=\angle APD$ (vertical angles), the total is $360^\circ=90\cdot4$.

**Answer: (C) 4**

amc12-ahsme-1972-21.title: A different crossing
amc12-ahsme-1972-21.body:
Let $G$ be where $AC$ crosses $BF$.
- $FGCE$ is a quadrilateral, so $\angle F+\angle C+\angle E+\angle FGC=360^\circ$.
- $AGBD$ is a concave quadrilateral (a dart) with its reflex angle at $G$, equal to $360^\circ-\angle AGB$. So $\angle A+\angle B+\angle D+(360^\circ-\angle AGB)=360^\circ$, i.e. $\angle A+\angle B+\angle D=\angle AGB$.

As $\angle AGB=\angle FGC$ (vertical angles), adding gives a total of $360^\circ$, so $n=4$.

**Answer: (C) 4**

amc12-ahsme-1972-22.title: Vieta
amc12-ahsme-1972-22.body:
Let the third root be $c$. The sum of roots is $0$ (no $x^2$ term), so $c=-2a$. Then $q$ = sum of products of pairs $=(a+bi)(a-bi)+c\big[(a+bi)+(a-bi)\big]=a^2+b^2+(-2a)(2a)=b^2-3a^2$.

**Answer: (E) $b^2-3a^2$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-23.title: Circle through the extreme corners
amc12-ahsme-1972-23.body:
Place the bottom two squares on $[0,2]\times[0,1]$ and the top square on $[\frac12,\frac32]\times[1,2]$. By symmetry the centre is $(1,h)$. The farthest points are the bottom corners $(0,0)$ and the top corners $(\frac12,2)$; the smallest circle passes through both: $1+h^2=\frac14+(2-h)^2\Rightarrow4h=\frac{13}{4}\Rightarrow h=\frac{13}{16}$. Radius $\sqrt{1+\frac{169}{256}}=\frac{\sqrt{425}}{16}=\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{16}$. (Moving the centre up or down would make one of these distances larger, so this is optimal.)

**Answer: (D) $\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{16}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-23.title: Compare to choices
amc12-ahsme-1972-23.body:
The corners $(0,0)$ and $(\frac32,2)$ are $\sqrt{2.25+4}=2.5$ apart, so any containing circle has radius at least $1.25$, ruling out (B). Radius exactly $1.25$ would force these two corners to be ends of a diameter, centre $(0.75,1)$, but then $(2,0)$ is $\sqrt{1.5625+1}\approx1.6>1.25$ away. So the radius exceeds $1.25$; $\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{16}\approx1.288$ works (all eight outer corners are within it) and is less than $\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{16}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-24.title: Two equations
amc12-ahsme-1972-24.body:
Rate $r$, time $t$. Faster: $\left(r+\frac12\right)\frac45t=rt\Rightarrow\frac45r+\frac25=r\Rightarrow r=2$. Slower: $\frac32\left(t+\frac52\right)=2t\Rightarrow\frac t2=\frac{15}4\Rightarrow t=7.5$. Distance $2\cdot7.5=15$.

**Answer: (B) 15**

amc12-ahsme-1972-25.title: Spot right triangles
amc12-ahsme-1972-25.body:
$25^2+60^2=625+3600=4225=65^2$ and $39^2+52^2=1521+2704=4225=65^2$. So the quadrilateral can be split by a diagonal of length $65$ into right triangles $25$-$60$-$65$ and $39$-$52$-$65$; its two opposite right angles add to $180^\circ$, so it is cyclic, and (a cyclic quadrilateral being determined by its consecutive sides) it is our quadrilateral. Each right angle subtends the diagonal, so the diagonal $65$ is a diameter.

**Answer: (C) 65**

amc12-ahsme-1972-25.title: Law of cosines
amc12-ahsme-1972-25.body:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between sides $25$ and $60$; the opposite angle (between $39$ and $52$) is $180^\circ-\theta$. Equate the diagonal: $25^2+60^2-3000\cos\theta=39^2+52^2+4056\cos\theta$, i.e. $4225-3000\cos\theta=4225+4056\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta=0$, $\theta=90^\circ$, the diagonal is $65$ and is a diameter.

**Answer: (C) 65**

amc12-ahsme-1972-26.title: Broken chord theorem
amc12-ahsme-1972-26.body:
Archimedes' broken chord theorem: if $M$ is the midpoint of arc $CAB$ (so $MC=MB$) and $MP\perp AB$, then $P$ is the midpoint of the broken chord $CAB$: $PB=CA+AP$. *Proof:* take $D$ on $PB$ with $PD=PA$; then $MD=MA$, and triangles $MAC$ and $MDB$ are congruent ($MC=MB$, $MA=MD$, $\angle MCA=\angle MBA$ inscribed on arc $MA$), so $DB=AC$. Thus $PB=PD+DB=AP+AC=(x+1)+x=2x+1$.

**Answer: (E) $2x+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-26.title: Sanity check with symmetry
amc12-ahsme-1972-26.body:
If $C$ approached $A$ ($x\to0$), $M$ would be the midpoint of arc $AB$ and $P$ the midpoint of $AB$, so $PB=AP=1$: only (E) gives $1$ at $x=0$.

**Answer: (E) $2x+1$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-27.title: Area formula
amc12-ahsme-1972-27.body:
$\sqrt{AB\cdot AC}=12$ so $AB\cdot AC=144$. Area $=\frac12AB\cdot AC\sin A=72\sin A=64$, so $\sin A=\frac89$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac89$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-27.title: Check
amc12-ahsme-1972-27.body:
$\frac89<1$ so such a triangle exists, e.g. $AB=AC=12$ with $\sin A=\frac89$, area $\frac12\cdot144\cdot\frac89=64$ ✓.

**Answer: (D) $\frac89$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-28.title: Count one quadrant
amc12-ahsme-1972-28.body:
Use squares of side $1$; the disc has radius $4$ centred at a grid corner. In one quadrant, the square $[i-1,i]\times[j-1,j]$ is covered iff its far corner satisfies $i^2+j^2\le16$. $i=1$: $j=1,2,3$; $i=2$: $j=1,2,3$; $i=3$: $j=1,2$; $i=4$: none. That is $8$ per quadrant, $32$ in all.

**Answer: (E) 32**

amc12-ahsme-1972-28.title: Row by row
amc12-ahsme-1972-28.body:
In the row at height $0$–$1$ from the centre, covered squares need $x\le\sqrt{16-1}\approx3.87$, so $3$ squares on each side; height $1$–$2$: $\sqrt{12}\approx3.46$, $3$ squares; height $2$–$3$: $\sqrt7\approx2.65$, $2$ squares; height $3$–$4$: $0$. Per half-row side: $3+3+2=8$; times $4$ = $32$.

**Answer: (E) 32**

amc12-ahsme-1972-30.title: Follow the folded corner
amc12-ahsme-1972-30.body:
The folded-over flap is a right triangle with hypotenuse $L$ (the crease) and angle $\theta$ at the top, so its bottom leg is $a=L\sin\theta$ (along the bottom edge from the crease's lower end to the corner) and makes angle $90^\circ-\theta$ with the crease. After folding, the bottom leg turns by $2(90^\circ-\theta)$, so it makes angle $2\theta$ with the bottom edge on the other side and reaches the left edge. The horizontal distance from the crease's lower end to the left edge is $6-a$, and $6-a=a\cos2\theta$. So $a(1+\cos2\theta)=6$, $a=\frac{6}{2\cos^2\theta}=3\sec^2\theta$, and $L=\frac{a}{\sin\theta}=3\sec^2\theta\csc\theta$.

**Answer: (A) $3\sec^2\theta\csc\theta$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-30.title: Check a case
amc12-ahsme-1972-30.body:
If $\theta=45^\circ$, the corner folds straight across: the flap leg $a$ satisfies $6-a=a\cos90^\circ=0$, so $a=6$ and $L=6\sqrt2$. (A): $3\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2=6\sqrt2$ ✓; (C): $3\cdot2=6$ ✗.

**Answer: (A) $3\sec^2\theta\csc\theta$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-32.title: Coordinates
amc12-ahsme-1972-32.body:
Power of a point: $CE\cdot ED=AE\cdot EB$, so $CE=\frac{12}{3}=4$. Put $E=(0,0)$, $A=(-2,0)$, $B=(6,0)$, $C=(0,4)$, $D=(0,-3)$. The centre is at $x=2$ (perpendicular bisector of $AB$) and $y=\frac12$ (of $CD$). Radius$^2=(2+2)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac{65}{4}$, diameter $\sqrt{65}$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{65}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-32.title: Perpendicular-chords identity
amc12-ahsme-1972-32.body:
For perpendicular chords meeting at $E$, $AE^2+EB^2+CE^2+ED^2=4R^2=(\text{diameter})^2$. Here $4+36+16+9=65$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{65}$**

amc12-ahsme-1972-33.title: Make the hundreds digit small
amc12-ahsme-1972-33.body:
Write the number $100a+10b+c$. The quotient is $1+\frac{99a+9b}{a+b+c}$. To minimise, take $a=1$ (the smallest hundreds digit) and $c=9$ (largest units digit, only in the denominator): $1+\frac{99+9b}{10+b}=1+9+\frac{9}{10+b}$, minimised by the largest $b$ allowed, $b=8$: $\frac{189}{18}=10.5$.

**Answer: (C) 10.5**

amc12-ahsme-1972-33.title: Compare candidates
amc12-ahsme-1972-33.body:
$\frac{189}{18}=10.5$, $\frac{198}{18}=11$, $\frac{179}{17}\approx10.53$, $\frac{289}{19}\approx15.2$. Nothing beats $10.5$, which is among the choices.

**Answer: (C) 10.5**

amc12-ahsme-1972-34.title: Eliminate Tom
amc12-ahsme-1972-34.body:
$t=2h-3d$. Substitute into $2h^3=3d^3+t^3$: $2h^3=3d^3+(2h-3d)^3=3d^3+8h^3-36h^2d+54hd^2-27d^3$, so $0=6h^3-36h^2d+54hd^2-24d^3$, i.e. $h^3-6h^2d+9hd^2-4d^3=0=(h-d)^2(h-4d)$. $h=d$ gives $t=-d$, impossible, so $h=4d$, $t=5d$. Relatively prime forces $d=1$: ages $1,5,4$ (Dick, Tom, Harry). Sum of squares $1+25+16=42$.

**Answer: (A) 42**

amc12-ahsme-1972-35.title: Track the rotations
amc12-ahsme-1972-35.body:
Each side of the square (length $4$) is covered in two moves: a $120^\circ$ turn about the vertex at the middle of the side (bringing the next vertex to the corner), then a $30^\circ$ turn about the corner vertex (bringing an edge onto the next side). The pivots cycle $B,P,A,B,P,A,\dots$. In the starting position $A$ is at corner $A$ and $B$ is the next pivot; this repeats only after $12$ sides ($24$ moves, three trips around): after $4$ sides $P$ is at corner $A$, after $8$ sides $B$ is, and only after $12$ is $A$ there again with $P$ back at its starting spot.

In $24$ moves each vertex is the pivot in $8$ of them — exactly $4$ of the $120^\circ$ turns and $4$ of the $30^\circ$ turns. So $P$ moves in $8$ turns of $120^\circ$ and $8$ of $30^\circ$, each on a circle of radius $2$:
$$2\left(8\cdot\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+8\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=2\cdot\tfrac{20\pi}{3}=\tfrac{40\pi}{3}.$$

**Answer: (D) $40\pi/3$**
